description: Joining NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Yaoundé! Looking for curious, motivated teammates with skills or interests in frontend/backend development, full-stack engineering, DevOps, data science, UI/UX design, and space science. All experience levels are welcome. Let's combine our skills, learn together, and build something amazing in 48 hours!
summary:
Outpost Zero is a free browser game where kids aged 7 to 12 train as junior astronauts, then command a lunar outpost for 30 simulated days. In Level 1, an optional Earth Training Academy gives short interactive lessons on energy, air, water recycling and growing food. In Level 2, players click each part of an isometric base and spend two action points a day on it, balancing energy, oxygen, water and food for a crew of four. Every choice costs something: shielding the crew from a solar storm can use up power or daily actions.

The game turns the challenge's real constraints of life support, power budgeting, food production and radiation protection into decisions with consequences. The solar storm incidents are based on NASA's DONKI space-weather database. All resource numbers are simplified game values, not NASA measurements.

It matters because understanding these trade-offs is the first step to understanding how crews survive far from home. It needs no download or account, and players are never blocked from the mission.
details:
WHAT IT IS

Outpost Zero is a free browser game for children aged 7 to 12, in two levels: an optional Earth Training Academy (Level 1) and a 30-day Lunar Outpost mission (Level 2). Both are in plain English. The lunar mission is open from the start, so no one is blocked by a rigid progression.

LEVEL 1: EARTH TRAINING ACADEMY

Players create a callsign and choose a role: Navigation, Engineering or Sciences. Short interactive lessons cover energy, air, water recycling and growing food. Each lesson is a micro-lesson followed by a scenario challenge with supportive feedback. Checkmarks track completed lessons. An optional multiple-choice knowledge exam awards an Earth badge for 80% or higher. Training and the exam can be skipped.

LEVEL 2: LUNAR OUTPOST ZERO

A briefing shows the starting resources and rules. A crew of four uses oxygen, water and food every day, and the commander has two action points a day. The mission screen shows an isometric base with a solar array, habitat pod, hydroponic greenhouse, crew quarters, rover and radio comms array. Clicking a building opens a panel with its details and actions. Resource bars, a science score and a radiation shielding status stay visible. A 30-day calendar shows completed and upcoming days, with checkpoints every 10 days. Scheduled incidents include a system fault on day 4 and solar storm alerts on days 12 and 22. During a storm, the player chooses between spending energy to charge radiation shields or moving the crew to an underground bunker at the cost of daily actions. Every choice costs something. The mission ends in success or failure.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA

The solar storm incidents are based on solar energetic particle events from NASA's DONKI database. [CONFIRM BEFORE SUBMITTING: the storm popup shows an archived real DONKI record (time, detecting instrument, linked flares and coronal mass ejections) that we saved ahead of time. It is archived, not live. If it only imitates DONKI alerts, replace this sentence with "inspired by".] DONKI records contain no dose or intensity value, so we do not show one or scale damage to it. All resource numbers and units in the game are simplified game values, not NASA measurements.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The game introduces how a base balances power, life support, food and radiation protection, and why no choice is free. The intended impact is that a young player meets each idea in training, then uses it under pressure in the mission. Optional training and a skippable exam let children of different reading levels take part. It needs no account or download.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

React, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, Tailwind CSS v4 and Lucide icons. The base view and backdrop are SVG. Progress and mission state use React context, and there is no backend or database. NASA's DONKI API was called once by a script to save data locally.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

Claude (Anthropic) and Gemini (Google) helped write and review code, draft text and design the interface. The team reviewed and edited the outputs. [If applicable: the base illustration was SI-generated and is labelled in the app.] No NASA logos or branding are used.

CREATIVITY

Players learn first, then apply it under pressure in a base they can click through. Every action costs something, and the game separates real NASA data from game rules, so players can see which is which.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Audience: plain language for ages 7 to 12. Honesty: no invented NASA figures, and archived data is not presented as live. Accessibility: keyboard use, and status shown with text as well as colour. Reliability: it runs offline once loaded. Scope: a small team with 48 hours, so features were cut to keep one complete, playable loop.
